title: Problem Introduction
content: Erdős Problem #419 asks: what is the set of limit points of τ((n+1)!)/τ(n!), where τ is the divisor function? Erdős-Graham-Ivić-Pomerance proved in 1996 that the answer is {1} ∪ {1 + 1/k : k ≥ 1} = {1, 2, 3/2, 4/3, ...}. When n+1 = pk for a large prime p, the ratio is approximately 1 + 1/k.
mathContext: The problem reduces to analyzing how τ(n!) changes when n increments by 1. Since (n+1)! = (n+1) · n!, the change in τ is controlled entirely by the prime factorization of n+1 and how it interacts with the existing prime factorization of n!.. Erdős and Graham posed this problem in their influential 1980 monograph 'Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory'. The complete solution came 16 years later in a joint paper with Ivić and Pomerance.. Prerequisites: Divisor function τ(n), Factorial prime factorization, Limit points of sequences. Cross-reference (erdos-415): Also studies consecutive values of arithmetic functions — ordering patterns rather than ratios. Cross-reference (stirling-formula): Stirling's approximation provides the growth rate of n!, relevant to understanding τ(n!) asymptotics

title: Divisor Function and Multiplicativity
content: τ(n) = n.divisors.card counts positive divisors of n. The multiplicative formula τ(n) = ∏ₚ (vₚ(n) + 1) decomposes the divisor count into prime power contributions. This formula is the foundation of the entire proof.
mathContext: Uses `Nat.divisors.card` for τ and states the multiplicative formula `tau_multiplicative_formula` as an axiom. The product runs over `n.primeFactors` with each factor `padicValNat p n + 1`.. The multiplicative formula transforms the ratio τ((n+1)!)/τ(n!) into a product over primes dividing n+1, since primes not dividing n+1 contribute the same to both factorials.. Prerequisites: Nat.divisors, padicValNat, Finset.prod. Cross-reference (erdos-414): Uses the same divisor function τ in h(n) = n + τ(n) orbit dynamics. Cross-reference (erdos-415): Uses τ as one of the four arithmetic functions whose ordering patterns satisfy the triple-log law

title: The Factorial Divisor Ratio
content: factorialDivisorRatio(n) = τ((n+1)!)/τ(n!) measures how the divisor count of factorials changes. This sequence has a rich but discrete set of limit points.
mathContext: Defined as a rational number `(tau (n + 1).factorial : ℚ) / (tau n.factorial : ℚ)` with a guard for zero factorials. Using ℚ avoids real number complications for this inherently rational quantity.. The ratio is always ≥ 1 since (n+1)! = (n+1) · n! and adding a factor can only increase or maintain divisor count. In fact, the ratio is strictly > 1 for n ≥ 1.

title: Legendre's Formula and Factorial Valuations
content: Legendre's formula: vₚ(n!) = Σᵢ≥₁ ⌊n/pⁱ⌋. This gives the exact p-adic valuation of n!, which controls each factor in the ratio formula. The lower bound vₚ(n!) ≥ n/p is used to show small primes contribute negligibly.
mathContext: Defines `padicValFactorial p n` as `∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, n / p^(i + 1)` and axiomatizes `legendre_formula` equating it with `padicValNat p n.factorial`. Also axiomatizes the lower bound `padic_factorial_lower_bound`.. Adrien-Marie Legendre derived this formula in 1808. It's equivalent to vₚ(n!) = (n - Sₚ(n))/(p - 1) where Sₚ(n) is the digit sum of n in base p.. Cross-reference (kummer-theorem): Kummer's theorem also uses Legendre's formula — the carry count in base-p addition equals digit sum differences via Legendre. Cross-reference (erdos-728-factorial-divisibility): Uses Legendre's formula for p-adic analysis of factorial divisibility conditions

title: The Ratio Product Formula
content: The key identity: τ((n+1)!)/τ(n!) = ∏_{p|n+1} (1 + vₚ(n+1)/(vₚ(n!)+1)). Using the multiplicativity τ(n) = ∏ₚ(vₚ(n)+1), the factorial ratio telescopes to a product over primes dividing n+1. Each factor measures how the exponent of p in the factorial increases.
mathContext: Axiomatized as `ratio_product_formula`: the ratio equals a `Finset.prod` over `(n + 1).primeFactors`. Each factor is `1 + vₚ(n+1) / (vₚ(n!) + 1)`. The denominator vₚ(n!) + 1 appears because τ counts vₚ + 1, not vₚ.. Proof method: Follows from the multiplicativity of τ: τ((n+1)!) / τ(n!) = ∏ₚ (vₚ((n+1)!) + 1) / (vₚ(n!) + 1). For p ∤ n+1, vₚ((n+1)!) = vₚ(n!) so the factor is 1. For p | n+1, vₚ((n+1)!) = vₚ(n!) + vₚ(n+1), giving the formula.. This decomposition is the key to the entire proof: it separates the ratio into contributions from individual primes, allowing separate analysis of small and large primes.

title: Small Primes Contribute ≈ 1
content: For primes p ≤ n^(2/3), the p-adic valuation vₚ(n!) is large (≈ n/p by Legendre's formula), so vₚ(n+1)/(vₚ(n!)+1) is small. The product over all small primes satisfies 1 ≤ contribution ≤ 1 + (log n)²/n^(1/3), which tends to 1 as n → ∞.
mathContext: Two axioms: `small_primes_contribution` gives the explicit bound 1 ≤ S ≤ 1 + (log n)²/n^(1/3), and `small_primes_limit` expresses the limit S → 1 using the ε-N formulation.. Proof method: For small p ≤ n^(2/3): vₚ(n+1) ≤ log₂(n) (since p^vₚ ≤ n+1), while vₚ(n!) ≥ n/p ≥ n^(1/3). So each factor is 1 + O(log n / n^(1/3)). With at most log₂(n) primes, the product is 1 + O((log n)² / n^(1/3)).. The threshold n^(2/3) is chosen so that small primes have negligible contribution while at most one prime can exceed the threshold. Any exponent in (1/2, 1) would work; 2/3 is a clean choice.

title: Large Prime Contribution
content: If p > n^(2/3) divides n+1, then p² > n+1 so vₚ(n+1) = 1. At most one such prime exists (since p > n^(2/3) means n+1/p < n^(1/3)). When n+1 = pk for large prime p, this prime's contribution dominates, giving ratio ≈ 1 + 1/k. When n+1 is prime (k=1), the ratio ≈ 2.
mathContext: Three axioms: `at_most_one_large_prime` bounds the count to ≤ 1, `large_prime_valuation` shows vₚ(n+1) = 1, and `prime_case` gives the ratio ≈ 2 when n+1 is prime. The contribution from a large prime p with n+1 = pk is (1 + 1/(vₚ(n!) + 1)) ≈ 1 + 1/k since vₚ(n!) ≈ k - 1.. Proof method: If p > n^(2/3) divides n+1, write n+1 = pk where k < n^(1/3). Then vₚ(n!) = ⌊n/p⌋ = k - 1 (since n = pk - 1). So the factor is (k - 1 + 1 + 1)/(k - 1 + 1) = (k + 1)/k ≈ 1 + 1/k.. The dichotomy: either n+1 has a large prime factor (giving limit point 1 + 1/k), or all prime factors are small (giving limit point 1). This exhaustive partition yields the complete set of limit points.

title: The Limit Point Set and Characterization
content: limitPointSet := {1} ∪ {1 + 1/k : k ≥ 1}. Three axioms establish the characterization: one_is_limit_point (1 is achieved by highly composite n+1), one_plus_reciprocal_is_limit_point (each 1+1/k is achieved by n+1 = pk), and only_these_limit_points (no other limit points exist). The sequence 1+1/k converges to 1, which is itself a limit point.
mathContext: Defines `limitPointSet` as `{1} ∪ {x | ∃ k : ℕ, k ≥ 1 ∧ x = 1 + 1 / k}`. Limit points are expressed via `∀ ε > 0, ∃ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, |factorialDivisorRatio n - x| < ε` using Mathlib's `Filter.Frequently`.. The set {1} ∪ {1 + 1/k : k ≥ 1} = {1, 2, 3/2, 4/3, 5/4, ...} is a countable closed set with 1 as its only accumulation point. It's topologically interesting: closed in ℝ, discrete except at 1, and bounded in [1, 2].. Prerequisites: Filter.atTop, Filter.Frequently (∃ᶠ), Set membership

title: Concrete Examples
content: When n+1 is prime: ratio ≈ 2 (the largest limit point). When n+1 = 2p: ratio ≈ 3/2. When n+1 = 3p: ratio ≈ 4/3. When n+1 is highly composite (smooth): ratio ≈ 1. These four cases illustrate the full range of limit points.
mathContext: Four axioms for concrete cases: `example_prime` (p-1 → 2), `example_twice_prime` (2p-1 → 3/2), `example_thrice_prime` (3p-1 → 4/3), `example_highly_composite` (smooth n+1 → 1). Each uses the large prime structure of n+1.. Proof method: For n+1 = kp with large prime p: the large prime factor p contributes ≈ 1 + 1/k, and small factors of k contribute ≈ 1. By Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, there are infinitely many such n for each k, ensuring each limit point is achieved infinitely often.

title: Sawhney's Characterization (Proved)
content: sawhney_characterization is a proved theorem giving the full iff: x is a limit point of factorialDivisorRatio ⟺ x ∈ limitPointSet. The forward direction uses only_these_limit_points; the reverse splits into the case x = 1 (using one_is_limit_point) and x = 1 + 1/k (using one_plus_reciprocal_is_limit_point).
mathContext: The proof uses pattern matching on `Set.mem_union`: `cases hx with | inl h1 => ... | inr hk => ...`. The forward direction is `only_these_limit_points x`, and the reverse direction dispatches on whether x = 1 or x = 1 + 1/k.. Proof method: Structural: the theorem is purely logical, combining three axioms into an iff. The mathematical content is in the axioms; this theorem packages them cleanly.. This is one of the few fully proved theorems in the file (not sorry'd or axiomatized). It demonstrates that the Lean formalization correctly captures the logical structure of the characterization.

title: Asymptotics of τ(n!)
content: τ(n!) grows extremely rapidly: at least 2^(n/log n). More precisely, log τ(n!) ~ n log n / log log n. These give context for why the ratio τ((n+1)!)/τ(n!) is close to 1 for most n — the factorial divisor count is so large that multiplying by n+1 barely changes it.
mathContext: Two axioms: `tau_factorial_growth` gives the lower bound τ(n!) ≥ 2^(n/log n), and `tau_factorial_log_asymptotic` gives log τ(n!) ~ n log n / log log n using the ε-N formulation.. Since log τ(n!) ~ n log n / log log n, the ratio τ((n+1)!)/τ(n!) = exp(log τ((n+1)!) - log τ(n!)) ≈ exp(O(log n / log log n)). For most n, the difference is small, pushing the ratio toward 1.. Cross-reference (stirling-formula): Stirling's formula gives log(n!) ~ n log n, while log τ(n!) ~ n log n / log log n — the extra log log n factor comes from the prime structure

title: Limit Set Properties
content: Proves three properties of the limit point set: (1) 1 ∈ limitPointSet, (2) 1 + 1/k ∈ limitPointSet for all k ≥ 1, (3) all elements are ≥ 1. The proof uses Set.mem_union for membership and linarith for the lower bound.
mathContext: The proof is fully constructive: membership via `left; rfl` and `right; use k, hk`, and the lower bound via `linarith` with `one_div_pos`. Uses pattern matching on `Set.mem_union` for case analysis.. Proof method: Direct proof with case splits. The lower bound x ≥ 1 follows because every element is either 1 or 1 + 1/k ≥ 1 for positive k.

title: Summary Theorem
content: erdos_419_summary combines three results into one: (1) sawhney_characterization — the complete iff characterization, (2) one_is_limit_point — 1 is a limit point, (3) one_plus_reciprocal_is_limit_point — each 1+1/k is a limit point. Proved by exact ⟨sawhney_characterization, one_is_limit_point, one_plus_reciprocal_is_limit_point⟩.
mathContext: Proved by anonymous constructor `⟨..., ..., ...⟩` combining the three component results. This is a packaging theorem that presents the complete solution in one statement.. Proof method: Direct: the proof is a single `exact` with a triple, extracting the three established results.. This is the definitive formalization of Erdős Problem #419. The solution is COMPLETE: the limit points are exactly {1} ∪ {1 + 1/k : k ≥ 1}, with the core mathematical arguments axiomatized and the logical structure proved.
